rows.label: Vernier calipers
rows.correct: measure external diameter, internal diameter and depth with appropriate jaws or depth rod
rows.explanation: The appropriate part of the instrument must contact the measured surface.

rows.label: Vernier least count
rows.correct: difference between one main-scale division and one vernier-scale division for a direct vernier
rows.explanation: The least count sets the resolution of a direct vernier.

rows.label: Corrected instrument reading
rows.correct: observed reading minus signed zero error
rows.explanation: A positive zero error must be subtracted.

rows.label: Screw-gauge pitch
rows.correct: axial distance moved by the screw in one complete rotation
rows.explanation: Pitch is divided by circular-scale divisions to obtain least count.

rows.label: Screw-gauge least count
rows.correct: pitch divided by number of circular-scale divisions
rows.explanation: Use consistent length units in this ratio.

rows.label: Screw-gauge ratchet
rows.correct: limits the force applied to the object
rows.explanation: It reduces errors due to excessive compression.

rows.label: Backlash error
rows.correct: lag caused by loose engagement of screw threads after reversing rotation
rows.explanation: Take final readings while turning in a consistent direction.

rows.label: Pendulum period measurement
rows.correct: time for many complete oscillations divided by their number
rows.explanation: Timing many oscillations reduces the fractional effect of reaction time.

rows.label: Small-angle pendulum T squared versus L plot
rows.correct: straight line with slope 4π²/g
rows.explanation: T² = 4π²L/g under the small-angle approximation.

rows.label: Damped pendulum amplitude
rows.correct: decreases as mechanical energy is dissipated
rows.explanation: Mechanical energy is lost to the surroundings through resistance.

rows.label: Principle of moments
rows.correct: clockwise and anticlockwise moments balance for rotational equilibrium
rows.explanation: A balanced metre scale can be used to compare masses using lever arms.

rows.label: Young modulus experiment
rows.correct: measure wire extension under a known load and use stress divided by strain
rows.explanation: Keep the load within the elastic limit.

rows.label: Capillary rise of wetting water
rows.correct: surface tension can be obtained from rise height, capillary radius, density and contact angle
rows.explanation: For a clean vertical tube, 2T cosθ = hρgr.

rows.label: Detergent in capillary experiment
rows.correct: generally reduces water surface tension
rows.explanation: The rise height changes when surface tension changes, with other conditions controlled.

rows.label: Terminal velocity experiment
rows.correct: viscous drag balances effective weight at terminal speed
rows.explanation: For a small sphere in the Stokes regime, viscosity follows from radius, densities and terminal speed.

rows.label: Resonance-tube successive resonances
rows.correct: length difference is half the sound wavelength
rows.explanation: The same end correction cancels in the difference of successive resonance lengths.

rows.label: Method of mixtures
rows.correct: heat lost by hotter bodies equals heat gained by cooler bodies and calorimeter in an insulated model
rows.explanation: Account for the calorimeter heat capacity when necessary.

rows.label: Metre-bridge balance
rows.correct: ratio of gap resistances equals ratio of corresponding balancing wire lengths
rows.explanation: Uniform wire and a null detector reading are required.

rows.label: Wire resistivity
rows.correct: resistance times cross-sectional area divided by length
rows.explanation: Measure wire diameter to obtain its cross-sectional area.

rows.label: Ohm-law V versus I graph
rows.correct: slope gives resistance of an ohmic conductor at fixed temperature
rows.explanation: Use potential difference on the vertical axis and current on the horizontal axis.

rows.label: Galvanometer half-deflection method
rows.correct: a suitable shunt is adjusted to halve the original deflection
rows.explanation: The method can estimate galvanometer resistance while accounting for circuit resistance.

rows.label: Removal of optical parallax
rows.correct: image and reference object do not shift relative to each other when the eye moves sideways
rows.explanation: This locates the image plane.

rows.label: Prism minimum deviation
rows.correct: angle of incidence equals angle of emergence for the symmetric ray path
rows.explanation: The internal refraction angles are both half the prism angle.

rows.label: Travelling-microscope glass-slab method
rows.correct: normal-view refractive index is real thickness divided by apparent thickness
rows.explanation: Refraction makes the viewed lower surface appear raised.

rows.label: Forward diode characteristic
rows.correct: current increases rapidly beyond the forward knee region
rows.explanation: The diode has a nonlinear current-voltage curve.

rows.label: Zener reverse breakdown
rows.correct: large reverse-current change occurs with relatively small voltage change in the breakdown region
rows.explanation: A series resistor limits current during measurement.

chemistry.name: p-Block Elements: Trends and First-Element Behaviour

rows.label: Group 13 valence configuration
rows.correct: ns²np¹
rows.explanation: There are three valence electrons in the general group 13 configuration.

rows.label: Group 14 valence configuration
rows.correct: ns²np²
rows.explanation: There are four valence electrons in the general group 14 configuration.

rows.label: Group 15 valence configuration
rows.correct: ns²np³
rows.explanation: There are five valence electrons in the general group 15 configuration.

rows.label: Group 16 valence configuration
rows.correct: ns²np⁴
rows.explanation: There are six valence electrons in the general group 16 configuration.

rows.label: Group 17 valence configuration
rows.correct: ns²np⁵
rows.explanation: There are seven valence electrons in the general group 17 configuration.

rows.label: Group 18 configuration except helium
rows.correct: ns²np⁶
rows.explanation: A filled valence shell is characteristic of noble gases other than helium.

rows.label: Helium configuration
rows.correct: 1s²
rows.explanation: The first shell is complete with two electrons.

rows.label: Atomic size down a p-block group
rows.correct: generally increases because additional electron shells are occupied
rows.explanation: Compare the same kind of atomic radius when making a trend.

rows.label: First ionisation enthalpy across a period
rows.correct: generally rises with effective nuclear charge, with configuration-related exceptions
rows.explanation: Subshell and pairing effects can produce local deviations.

rows.label: Electronegativity down a p-block group
rows.correct: generally decreases as atomic size and shielding increase
rows.explanation: This is a general trend rather than a rule without exceptions.

rows.label: Inert-pair effect
rows.correct: increasing reluctance of the outer ns² pair to participate in bonding in heavier elements
rows.explanation: It helps stabilise oxidation states two units below the group maximum.

rows.label: Group 13 lower oxidation state
rows.correct: +1 becomes more stable toward the heavier members
rows.explanation: The inert-pair effect favours retention of the ns² pair.

rows.label: Group 14 lower oxidation state
rows.correct: +2 is relatively more stable for heavier members than for lighter members
rows.explanation: Lead commonly shows a stable +2 state.

rows.label: Group 15 lower oxidation state
rows.correct: +3 gains relative stability compared with +5 down the group
rows.explanation: This is associated with the inert-pair effect.

rows.label: Small size of the first p-block member
rows.correct: contributes to its anomalous behaviour relative to heavier congeners
rows.explanation: High charge density affects bonding and physical properties.

rows.label: Second-period octet restriction
rows.correct: second-period central atoms do not expand their valence octet
rows.explanation: Boron, carbon, nitrogen, oxygen and fluorine lack an available third shell in the standard valence model.

rows.label: Carbon catenation
rows.correct: strong carbon-carbon bonds support extensive chains and rings
rows.explanation: Catenation is the ability to form bonds to atoms of the same element.

rows.label: Carbon versus silicon multiple bonding
rows.correct: carbon forms strong pπ-pπ multiple bonds more readily
rows.explanation: The compact second-period orbitals overlap more effectively.

rows.label: Nitrogen molecule
rows.correct: contains a strong N≡N triple bond
rows.explanation: This contributes to the low reactivity of nitrogen under ordinary conditions.

rows.label: Nitrogen versus phosphorus valence
rows.correct: nitrogen does not form a neutral pentahalide analogous to PCl₅ in the octet model
rows.explanation: Nitrogen cannot accommodate ten electrons in its second-shell valence region.

rows.label: Oxygen versus sulfur molecular form
rows.correct: oxygen commonly occurs as O₂ whereas sulfur commonly occurs as S₈
rows.explanation: Differences in bonding favour different elemental molecular structures.

rows.label: Fluorine oxidation state in compounds
rows.explanation: Fluorine is the most electronegative element and does not show positive oxidation states in its compounds.

rows.label: Halogen elemental molecules
rows.correct: diatomic X₂ molecules
rows.explanation: Group 17 elements occur in paired elemental molecules under usual molecular conditions.

rows.label: Chlorine versus fluorine electron gain enthalpy
rows.correct: chlorine has a more negative first electron gain enthalpy
rows.explanation: Small fluorine orbitals increase repulsion for an added electron.

rows.label: Noble-gas low ordinary reactivity
rows.correct: filled valence shells and high ionisation enthalpies
rows.explanation: Heavier members can form compounds under suitable conditions.

rows.label: Metallic character down p-block groups
rows.correct: generally increases
rows.explanation: Larger atoms tend to lose valence electrons more readily.

rows.label: Acidity of main-group oxides across a period
rows.correct: generally increases as nonmetallic character increases
rows.explanation: Metallic oxides tend to be basic whereas many nonmetal oxides are acidic.

rows.label: Boron bonding tendency
rows.correct: predominantly covalent compounds rather than simple B³⁺ salts
rows.explanation: The small atom and high ionisation requirements disfavour formation of a simple B³⁺ ion.

rows.label: Crystallisation
rows.correct: purifies a solid using different solubilities in hot and cold solvent
rows.explanation: The desired solid crystallises on cooling while many soluble impurities remain in solution.

rows.label: Simple distillation
rows.correct: separates a volatile liquid from nonvolatile impurities or liquids with widely separated boiling points
rows.explanation: Vapour is condensed to collect the volatile component.

rows.label: Fractional distillation
rows.correct: separates miscible liquids with relatively close boiling points
rows.explanation: A fractionating column provides repeated vapour-liquid equilibration.

rows.label: Steam distillation
rows.correct: isolates a steam-volatile substance immiscible with water
rows.explanation: The mixture can distil below the boiling point of the organic component alone.

rows.label: Sublimation
rows.correct: separates a sublimable solid from nonsublimable impurities
rows.explanation: The volatile solid passes through vapour and is deposited on cooling.

rows.label: Chromatography
rows.correct: separates components by different distribution between stationary and mobile phases
rows.explanation: Different affinities produce different migration speeds.

rows.label: Rf in planar chromatography
rows.correct: distance travelled by solute divided by distance travelled by solvent front
rows.explanation: Both distances are measured from the origin.

rows.label: Lassaigne sodium fusion
rows.correct: converts covalently bound heteroatoms into water-soluble ionic salts
rows.explanation: The extract can then be tested for nitrogen, sulfur and halogens.

rows.label: Nitrogen in Lassaigne extract
rows.correct: cyanide can lead to Prussian-blue formation after the appropriate iron-ion treatment
rows.explanation: The procedure requires the specified reagents and suitable acidification.

rows.label: Sulfur with sodium nitroprusside
rows.correct: violet colour
rows.explanation: Sulfide in the fusion extract gives the characteristic response.

rows.label: Nitrogen and sulfur together in sodium fusion
rows.correct: thiocyanate can give a blood-red colour with ferric ions
rows.explanation: The response arises from an iron-thiocyanate complex.

rows.label: Halogen testing in sodium-fusion extract
rows.correct: acidify and boil with nitric acid before adding silver nitrate
rows.explanation: This removes interfering cyanide and sulfide under the prescribed procedure.

rows.label: Silver chloride precipitate
rows.correct: white and soluble in dilute aqueous ammonia
rows.explanation: Complex formation dissolves AgCl under the usual test conditions.

rows.label: Silver bromide precipitate
rows.correct: pale yellow and dissolves in concentrated aqueous ammonia
rows.explanation: It is less readily dissolved than AgCl.

rows.label: Silver iodide precipitate
rows.correct: yellow and insoluble in aqueous ammonia in the standard test
rows.explanation: Its low solubility resists dissolution in this test.

rows.label: Carbylamine test
rows.correct: primary amines form foul-smelling isocyanides with chloroform and alcoholic KOH
rows.explanation: Secondary and tertiary amines do not give the standard positive test.

rows.label: Neutral ferric chloride with phenol
rows.correct: may produce a characteristic coloured complex
rows.explanation: This is a common test for the phenolic group.

rows.label: 2,4-DNP test
rows.correct: aldehydes and ketones form coloured hydrazone precipitates
rows.explanation: It detects the carbonyl group of these compounds.

rows.label: Tollens test with an aldehyde
rows.correct: silver is deposited from the ammoniacal silver reagent
rows.explanation: The aldehyde is oxidised while silver ions are reduced.

rows.label: Sodium bicarbonate with a carboxylic acid
rows.correct: carbon dioxide effervescence
rows.explanation: A carboxylic acid is strong enough to liberate CO₂ from bicarbonate.

rows.label: Bromine test for alkene unsaturation
rows.correct: bromine colour disappears under the standard addition-test conditions
rows.explanation: Interpret the result with other possible bromine-reactive groups in mind.

rows.label: Carbonate anion with dilute acid
rows.correct: releases carbon dioxide that turns limewater milky
rows.explanation: The gas forms calcium carbonate in limewater.

rows.label: Sulfide anion with dilute acid
rows.correct: can release hydrogen sulfide
rows.explanation: The gas darkens suitable lead-acetate paper by forming lead sulfide.

rows.label: Sulfate with barium chloride after acidification
rows.correct: white barium sulfate precipitate persists in dilute acid
rows.explanation: Acidification helps exclude carbonate interference.

rows.label: Ammonium ion with warm aqueous base
rows.correct: ammonia is released
rows.explanation: The gas turns moist red litmus blue.

rows.label: Copper(II) with excess aqueous ammonia
rows.correct: deep-blue complex solution
rows.explanation: Excess ammonia coordinates to the copper ion.

rows.label: Ferric ion with thiocyanate
rows.correct: blood-red solution under suitable conditions
rows.explanation: A coloured iron-thiocyanate complex forms.

rows.label: Aluminium hydroxide amphoterism
rows.correct: dissolves in both acid and excess strong base
rows.explanation: The hydroxide can form soluble species in either medium.

rows.label: Oxalic-acid versus permanganate titration
rows.correct: warm acidic conditions facilitate the redox reaction
rows.explanation: The standard procedure uses dilute sulfuric acid and appropriate warming.

rows.label: Permanganate titration endpoint
rows.correct: first faint pink colour persisting after mixing
rows.explanation: Permanganate serves as its own indicator. Non-endpoint permanganate is reduced.

rows.label: Strong acid versus strong base titration
rows.correct: equivalence is near pH 7 at 25 °C in the dilute ideal model
rows.explanation: Neutralisation consumes equivalent amounts of H⁺ and OH⁻.

rows.label: Enthalpy of neutralisation of dilute strong acid and base
rows.correct: approximately −57 kJ per mole of water formed
rows.explanation: This approximates H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) forming water.

rows.label: Lyophilic sol preparation
rows.correct: a material with strong affinity for the dispersion medium forms a sol readily
rows.explanation: Starch sols illustrate a lyophilic preparation.

rows.label: Lyophobic sol preparation
rows.correct: a dispersed material with little affinity for the medium requires a suitable preparation method
rows.explanation: Ferric hydroxide sol can be prepared by controlled hydrolysis.
